rv.q: It's an absolute thrill to watch this innovative company bring a great novel to life.
Ulysses is a bold production that both enlightens and challenges us to wander, sometimes aimlessly, through the world that James Joyce left for us to decipher.
Elevator Repair Service’s Ulysses is both a fun night at the theatre and a cultural outing that may make you feel smarter, but it is not invested in these questions.
Strangers to Ulysses may simply want to sit back and enjoy the performances as they occur—like admiring the portraits in a madhouse Dublin gallery—and not worry about the narrative.
Good theatre holds you in a present moment that is not your own, and Ulysses really demands that you stick with it and stay there.
Just sit back, relax, and enjoy the wild, unpredictable shenanigans as ERS celebrates another literary treasure as only it can.
While the play does not substitute for the book’s puns, wordplays and walking tour of Dublin, this is a trenchant stage version of Joyce’s novel that can be digested in one sitting.
The adaptation succeeds as a celebration of Joyce's antic imagination and the idiosyncratic spirit of ERS's determination to bring modernist writers to the stage.
The production doesn't demand that you have the 'correct' response to Joyce; it makes space for whatever vision of the text you can construct from its fragments.
I was never attached to the this production’s story or the outcome, and this may be exactly what James intended.
But this feels more like gloss than adaptation, an exercise that captures elements of the source material without ever standing on its own terms.
Fortunately, the majority of Joyce’s narrative is rendered with humor, passion, and imagination.
The seven-person ensemble undertakes dozens of roles, and while plenty of captivating moments surface, the whole fails to be greater than the parts.

Even when things go awry, they are skilled artists, but they are no match for the mandarin, willful, authoritative James Joyce, whose novel continues to fascinate and confound a century after its publication.
The Elevator Repair Service's production feels more like gloss than adaptation, an exercise that captures elements of Joyce without ever standing on its own terms.
